newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, buoyed by polls, in countdown to election.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, buoyed by polls, in countdown to election.

text.p: Blending sentimentality with hard-nosed political moves, President Bill Clinton sprinted toward Tuesday's election on Monday, confident he was poised to become the first Democrat to win a second term in 60 years.

Speaking to a fired-up crowd that filled a sports arena on the Cleveland State University campus, he urged his supporters to be sure to vote. "Are you ready for tomorrow? Will you be there?" he shouted, getting an affirmative roar in response.
Clinton said his contest with Republican rival Bob Dole would give voters a choice to determine "how we will go forward into the 21st century."
"It's about whether we will go forward on our own, or go forward together," he said. "You must seize the day to say this is our country, this is our future and we're going to build it together."

When a small group of Dole supporters tried to heckle the president, he shushed the crowd when it started to boo. "Don't boo them -- you'll only encourage them. Make them feel welcome. We're not like the other side -- in our America, we're not leaving anyone out," he said.

Clinton, giddy with nervous excitement and bleary-eyed from lack of sleep, flew to Cleveland from a Manchester, New Hampshire, reunion with old friends and supporters at Merrimack Restaurant, where he often ate breakfast during the 1992 New Hampshire primary campaign.

His eyes filled with tears as he greeted Michael Morrison, 20, a wheelchair-bound victim of cerebral palsy who helped put him on the road to the White House four years ago. Stooping to hug his loyal campaign worker, Clinton said: "How's it going, buddy? Good to see you."
Later, in a speech to a crowd huddled in bone-chilling weather outside the restaurant, Clinton said New Hampshire and the country did not have to take a gamble on him, as was the case four years ago.

"You know that compared to four years ago, in terms of the economy, the lowest crime rate in 10 years, declining welfare rolls, rising child support collection, in almost every way of indicating the character of American life, we are moving forward," he said.
"Are we going to finish the job?" Clinton asked rhetorically. "Your vote will decide."
He repeated a folksy assurance he gave New Hampshire voters in 1992 -- that he would be with them "till the last dog dies" -- and added: "Well folks, there's a lot of life left in this old dog."
Joining Clinton at his Cleveland campaign stop was Vice President Al Gore, who pushed for the election of a Democratic Congress.

"Don't let the Republicans fool you as they try to separate themselves from (Republican House Speaker) Newt Gingrich and Bob Dole," said Gore. Hillary Rodham Clinton and Tipper Gore joined their husbands at the rally, which was designed to cement a Clinton victory in Ohio.
No Republican has ever won the presidency without carrying the state.

From Cleveland, Clinton hopscotched by jet across the Midwest, stopping in Lexington, Kentucky, before going on to Des Moines, Iowa, and Sioux Falls, South Dakota. He was to end his long journey well after midnight in Little Rock, Arkansas, where he will vote on Tuesday.

Along his motorcade route to a rally in Lexington, Clinton was greeted by Kentucky tobacco producers protesting his moves to regulate cigarettes. "Keep FDA (Food and Drug Administration) off the farm," said signs on more than two dozen trucks parked along the highway.

The Clinton camp was confident the election would make him the first Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt in 1936 to win a second consecutive term and the mood aboard the president's plane was euphoric, like a winning team's locker room.

Clinton aides privately predicted he would defeat Dole in every one of the states on the final swing and said he was going to two of them -- Iowa and South Dakota -- only to help Democratic candidates for the Senate.

They said the only question was whether he would get a majority of the popular vote, improving on his 43 percent plurality in 1992 when he defeated then-President George Bush. "We're right on the edge" of a majority, one aide said.
